AQWA: Companies that supply clean water: utilities that treat and deliver it, plus makers of pipes, pumps, meters and treatment equipment. Industrials and utilities split the fund, making it a steadier infrastructure-style theme than most single-industry bets.
ASEC: Securitized bonds backed by less common loan types: aircraft and equipment leases, consumer loans, cell tower leases and data infrastructure. It looks for investment grade income away from plain mortgages and corporate bonds, so the holdings take effort to evaluate.
BSCA: Investment grade corporate bonds that all mature in 2036, bought and held until the fund itself winds down that year. It behaves much like owning a single long-term bond: steady interest, a known end date, and plenty of price movement when rates change.
BWTG: Large and mid-sized growth companies chosen from a model portfolio of the stocks that professional investors rate most highly for shareholder value. The mix roams across technology, energy, real estate and industry, so it looks quite different from a standard growth fund.
CANQ: Mostly bond funds holding mortgage bonds, high yield debt, government bonds and collateralized loans, combined with Nasdaq-100 equity exposure and options. The blend is shaped to behave like convertible bonds, offering stock-linked upside with bond-like income, though it owns few convertibles directly.
CEW: A bet on emerging market currencies against the US dollar, built with currency contracts while the cash sits in Treasury bills. It gains when currencies from Latin America, Asia and other emerging markets strengthen, and it can fall quickly when investors flee to the dollar.
CPNQ: Options on the Nasdaq-100 structured to protect against losses over a one-year period ending in December, while taking part in gains up to a cap. It trades away the biggest rallies in exchange for a much softer landing when tech stocks fall.
CVNY: An options strategy built around a single stock, Carvana, the online used-car seller, using synthetic covered calls to generate income. It pays regular distributions from selling those options, but gains are capped and a sharp drop in the stock hits the fund hard.
DDXX: A basket of broad equity funds covering value stocks, low-volatility stocks, small companies and international markets, assembled by a rules-based discipline process. It aims to beat a plain market-weighted stock fund by tilting toward steadier corners of the market.
DECO: Companies in the crypto business, including bitcoin miners, trading platforms, and chip and software firms, plus some direct bitcoin and ether exposure through futures and exchange-traded products. It captures the industry around crypto rather than one coin, and it is highly volatile.
DFII: Options contracts that give bitcoin exposure, combined with an income strategy that sells options to generate regular payouts. It offers a way to follow bitcoin with steadier cash flow, though bitcoin's sharp swings still drive the results.
DLNV: Options on the S&P 500 arranged to gain when the market moves up or down by a moderate amount over a one-year period ending each November. It is built for sideways or mildly trending markets, while a sharp move in one direction can leave it behind.
DRAI: A tactical mix of other funds spanning US stocks, bonds, gold and leveraged index funds, shifted by an artificial intelligence model toward whatever looks most attractive. Because it can lean on leveraged funds, its risk level can change quickly from cautious to aggressive.
DRGN: Chinese companies building generative artificial intelligence, from chip designers and server makers to internet platforms, with technology making up over three quarters of the fund. It is a focused bet on China's AI industry, so it swings sharply with sentiment toward Chinese tech.
DRKY: A concentrated portfolio of growth companies picked by a rules-based macro index, heaviest in health care and technology, layered with an options program that sells contracts for income. It targets a 15 percent annual distribution rate, and the concentrated holdings mean single stocks can move it a lot.
DTAN: Large companies outside the US picked as undervalued once intangible assets like patents, brands and research are counted alongside factories and cash. Health care and technology lead the mix, and the intangible lens means it can favor very different stocks than a traditional value fund.
ENHI: Large companies across developed markets outside the US, spread across financials, industrials, technology and health care, picked actively while keeping overall risk close to the broad international market. It suits a core international holding, with stock picks meant to add a modest edge.
EUIG: Investment grade corporate bonds from across Europe, issued in euros but hedged back into US dollars. It pays interest income from big European companies while the currency hedge removes most of the euro's ups and downs from the result.
EVLU: Value-priced stocks across emerging markets, with technology the biggest slice at over two fifths thanks to Asian chip and electronics makers, and a quality screen on top. It looks for bargains in developing economies, which adds currency and political risk to the value hunt.
GGM: A fund of sector funds that rotates among industries like energy, staples, utilities and technology based on macroeconomic signals. The whole mix can shift as the outlook changes, so it is an active bet on the managers' reading of the economy.
IBFR: Developed-market stocks outside the US, spread across banks, industry, technology and health care, paired with options that buffer the first 10 percent of losses. It aims for international growth with a softer landing in sell-offs, at the cost of some upside.
JELH: Income built from equity-linked notes, options and swaps tied to stocks and stock indexes, rather than from simply owning shares. It aims for high regular payouts, and the structured payoff means returns can behave quite differently from the stock market.
MCH: Actively managed Chinese stocks across Hong Kong, mainland and US listings, led by financials, with technology, internet and consumer companies behind. The managers hunt for companies that can keep growing for years, making it a core China holding with the usual political and currency risks.
MFLX: Municipal bonds from states, cities and agencies across the US, reaching into lower-rated high yield munis as well as solid investment grade ones. The interest is exempt from federal income tax, and the flexible mandate lets the managers chase higher yields.
MPIM: Exposure to a structured autocall index built on US momentum stocks, gained through swap contracts rather than owning shares directly. It is designed to pay regular income and can end early when conditions are met, but the payoff depends on the index staying above set levels.
NBFR: Exposure to the Nasdaq-100's big technology and growth companies, combined with options designed to buffer the first 10 percent of losses. It suits investors who want tech-led growth with a cushion, though gains are reduced by the cost of that protection.
NEWZ: US companies of all sizes chosen by an artificial intelligence system that scores the sentiment of news coverage about each stock. Financials and technology lead the current mix, and the lineup changes as news flow shifts, so it can turn over quickly.
PCEB: Below-investment-grade corporate bonds issued in Europe and denominated in euros, actively chosen for their higher yields. Along with the usual junk bond default risk, its results depend on the euro's value, since the bonds pay and trade in euros.
PCHI: High yield corporate bonds, the below-investment-grade debt often called junk bonds, chosen actively by Polen's credit team. It aims to beat the broader high yield market over a full credit cycle, accepting default risk in exchange for higher interest income.
PCLO: The safest slices, rated AAA, of collateralized loan obligations backed by private company loans. It offers income from private credit with the protection of sitting at the top of the payment line, though the underlying loans are not traded publicly.
PEZ: Consumer companies selling discretionary goods and services, from online retail and airlines to hotels, restaurants and carmakers, chosen for strong recent price momentum. The momentum focus means the lineup changes as trends shift, and it can lag when out-of-favor stocks suddenly rebound.
PSCM: Small US materials companies: chemical makers, metal miners, packaging, paper and specialty materials producers. It is a narrow bet on the raw-materials economy through small stocks, so it tends to swing hard with commodity prices and factory demand.
QSIX: Stocks from the Nasdaq-100, mostly big technology names, paired with futures contracts tied to the dividends those companies pay. It aims for stock growth plus a multiplied dividend stream, so the income side is amplified well beyond what the stocks alone would pay.
QTAP: Options on the Nasdaq-100 that aim to deliver accelerated gains up to a preset cap over a one-year period starting each April. It is a leveraged-style bet on big tech rising, and losses are not cushioned when the index falls.
QTUP: Small, specialized companies whose business is mainly quantum computing, from hardware builders to software and encryption firms. It is a pure-play bet on an early-stage technology, so holdings are mostly young companies and the price can swing violently.
RWIN: Large and mid-sized companies in developed markets outside the US, chosen with a next-generation multifactor process that blends traits like value, quality and momentum. Financials lead the mix, and the factor tilts mean it will not mirror a plain international index fund.
SCLZ: Dividend-paying US companies, mostly large and mid-sized, with technology the biggest slice at about two fifths of the fund. It aims for growing dividend income with growth potential, and its tech weight makes it livelier than a traditional dividend fund.
SIOO: The hundred largest US companies, spanning technology, banks, health care and consumer brands, paired with an options overlay that sells contracts for income. It targets an annual distribution rate of 15 percent, trading some upside in strong rallies for steady payouts.
TAGS: Futures contracts on four farm commodities, corn, wheat, soybeans and sugar, held through four sister funds in roughly equal parts. It gives broad exposure to crop and food prices in one fund, and futures-based returns can differ from spot commodity prices over time.
TDEM: Bonds from emerging market governments and companies across Latin America, Asia, Europe, Africa and the Middle East, actively managed as conditions change. It pays higher interest than developed-market debt, with extra risk from weaker economies and political turmoil.
TMNL: Long-term municipal bonds issued by cities, states and agencies across the US, paying interest that is exempt from federal income tax. Because the bonds mature far in the future, the price moves more than shorter muni funds when interest rates change.
TSYX: Leveraged daily exposure to an S&P 500 option income fund, aiming to amplify its daily move rather than match it one for one. The leverage resets every day, so it is a tool for very short holding periods and can drift badly in choppy markets.
UXOC: Options on the S&P 500 that aim to accelerate gains without an upside cap over a one-year period ending each October. It is built for strong bull markets, and it carries full exposure to losses when the market falls instead.
WDE: Securitized debt: bundles of commercial mortgages, car loans, equipment leases and similar loans packaged into bonds. It hunts for income in corners of the bond market beyond plain corporate and government debt, so it depends heavily on borrowers keeping up their payments.
WTLS: A long and short portfolio of US stocks, holding companies it favors while betting against others, combined with a straightforward long-only stock sleeve. It aims for stock-like returns with smaller swings, and it can trail badly when the market races upward.
XLSI: Consumer staples companies from the S&P 500, the makers of food, drinks, household and personal products, paired with an options overlay that collects premium income. Staples are a defensive corner of the market, and the options add payouts in exchange for some upside.
XTJA: Options on the S&P 500 that aim to deliver accelerated gains, magnifying the index's rise up to a preset cap, over a one-year period starting each January. The flip side is full exposure to losses, so it suits short, confident bets on a rising market.
XYZY: An options strategy on a single company, Block, the payments firm behind Square and Cash App, using synthetic covered calls to produce income. Distributions can be high, but gains are capped and the fund rides one volatile fintech stock.
YFFI: A yield-focused mix of corporate bonds, Treasury securities, asset-backed bonds and preferred shares, spread across many issuers. It is built to pay steady interest income as a core bond holding, with more credit risk than a Treasury-only fund carries.
YLDY: Large US companies, led by technology, paired with an options program that sells index contracts to turn part of the market's movement into income. It aims for high regular payouts, and the options overlay means it keeps less of the gain in strong rallies.
